result:
Solutions 1 and 2 are wrong, and Solution 3 is the only one whose answer is consistent with a valid counterexample.

**Solutions 1 and 2 fail at n = 8.** Let H be the Steiner quadruple system SQS(8), the 14 planes of AG(3,2) viewed as 4-sets. Every triple lies in exactly one block, so δ₃(H) = 1 and H is a {4}-graph, hence a {1,2,3,4}-graph. Take any 5-set F. Counting incidences shows F contains exactly one block B, and F \ B = {x} for a single vertex x. In any cyclic ordering of F, the two consecutive triples avoiding x both lie inside B. Each of these triples lies only in B, so they cannot receive distinct hyperedges. Hence H has no Berge-C₅³. Since 5 ≤ 8, the required property fails at n = 8, so n₀ ≥ 9. This rules out both 6 and 7.

**Solution 3 is consistent.** It gives n₀ = 9 with the SQS(8) counterexample at n = 8, which I verified. Its claim that n ≥ 9 works is a heuristic sketch, not a full proof. As a plausibility check, the blocking inequality it uses for 5-cycles holds with equality at n = 8 and fails for n = 9 and beyond, and a 9-vertex attempt to block C₅ by adding a vertex to SQS(8) can be routed around. I did not verify every t for all n ≥ 9, so 9 is the answer I'm fairly confident in rather than one I have proven.

CHOICE: 3
